hook.text: Here are three distributions, each drawn on its own axis. They look alike.

apart.text: And mixing them up is how confidence intervals get misread. So let's pull them apart.

pop.text: The first is the population. Here, that's what a million customers spend.

center.text: They spend fifty dollars on average, with a spread of eighteen.

unknown.text: It's wide, it's fixed... and in real life, you almost never get to see it.

sample.text: The second is one sample. Pick forty customers at random.

snapshot.text: It's a noisy snapshot of the population. Ragged, but about as wide, with a spread of about twenty.

data.text: That's what a histogram of your data shows. Raw values, one per customer.

third.text: The third is a different kind of thing. Average those forty, and you get one number... about forty-seven dollars.

block.text: That average becomes one block in a new chart.

repeat.text: Now pick forty more, and forty more. Five thousand samples later,

pile.text: the averages have piled up right on fifty. And their spread is under three dollars.

compare.text: On their own axes, these three looked alike. On one axis, the widths tell them apart.

raw.text: The population and the sample are raw values, spread across tens of dollars.

statistic.text: The third is a statistic, one average per sample. And it barely moves.

why.text: That gap is why forty customers can pin down the average of a million. And a histogram of your data? It's always the middle one.

trap.text: Now, here's a trap. A simulation has two ways to get more data... more samples, or bigger ones.

more.text: Draw more samples, from five hundred up to thirty-two thousand, and the histogram just gets smoother. Its spread stays near two point eight.

bigger.text: Make each sample bigger, from ten customers up to six hundred and forty, and the spread falls, from five and a half to under one.

real.text: And in real life, you only ever get ONE sample. Its size is the lever you actually control.

any.text: One last thing. The mean isn't special. Every statistic has a sampling distribution.

kinds.text: Take samples of sixty from a lopsided population, like incomes, and keep each sample's mean, median and maximum.

own.text: Each gets its own center, its own width, and its own shape. The maximum lands far out, wide and lopsided.

name.text: And that width, how far a statistic moves from one sample to the next, has a name... the standard error.
